claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating can be used to investigate nanoparticle thermal behavior at atomic scale.
In situ aberration-corrected TEM heating can be used to investigate the thermal behavior of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Atomic-resolution heating microscopy can reveal surface phase separation and surface-layer melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles is size-dependent.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo structural changes at lower temperatures than larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
An increased surface-to-volume ratio accelerates atomic diffusion in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on SiN TEM membranes.
The proposed heating experiment spans approximately ambient temperature to 973 K or higher.
The proposed experiment is conducted under high vacuum.
The experiment compares particles ranging from below 10 nm to tens of nanometers.
Pronounced atomic diffusion can drive progressive temperature-induced phase separation in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The relevant enhanced diffusion in smaller FeCuCrCoNi particles is specifically surface atomic diffusion caused by their high surface-to-volume ratio.
Higher surface energy in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles causes an earlier onset of structural instability.
The larger cores of larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles provide additional thermal stabilization.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will show surface reconstruction, phase segregation, or melting at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Ambient atmosphere or additional processing can alter the proposed size-dependent thermal behavior.
The onset temperature of structural change can be measured as a function of particle size using images and diffraction patterns acquired during heating.
Failure to observe lower transition temperatures in smaller particles would falsify the proposed directional size effect.
